title: Squashing Commits
description: Use the squash action in interactive rebase to combine multiple small commits into clean, meaningful ones.

data.text: Squashing combines multiple commits into one, merging their changes and messages. It is the most common interactive rebase operation and the primary tool for producing clean commit histories before merging to main.

When you mark a commit as squash, Git combines its changes with the previous commit. Git then opens your editor with the combined messages from both commits. You edit the message into a single clean message and save.

data.title: Squash commits with interactive rebase
data.code:
# Start interactive rebase on the last 4 commits
git rebase -i HEAD~4

# In the editor, change:
#   pick abc1234 feat(auth): add login endpoint
#   squash def5678 fix(auth): typo in login message
#   squash ghi9012 fix(auth): edge case
#   pick jkl3456 feat(api): add profile route

# Git opens editor with combined messages — edit into one clean message

data.title: Squash preserves the original author
data.text: When you squash, Git preserves the original author of all commits in the Author: trailer of the combined message. This maintains proper attribution in the Git history.

The fixup action is like squash, but Git automatically discards the fixup commit's message. Combined with the --autosquash flag, Git will automatically move fixup commits next to the commit they fix and mark them as fixup in the todo list.

data.title: Create fixup and squash commits
data.code:
# Commit a quick fix that should be squashed into a previous commit
git commit --fixup HEAD~2

# Git creates a commit with message: fixup! feat(auth): add login endpoint

# Rebase with --autosquash to apply the fixup
git rebase -i --autosquash HEAD~3

# Git automatically moves the fixup commit next to the target and marks it as 'fixup'

data.text: Squash vs fixup: when to use each

items: **squash** — When both commits have meaningful messages worth combining into one
**fixup** — When the second commit is purely a correction and its message is irrelevant
**--autosquash** — Automates placing fixup commits next to their targets in the todo list

data.text: The most common squash pattern is combining a chain of wip, fix, and test commits from a feature branch into a single clean commit before merging. Another pattern is grouping dependency updates into one commit to reduce noise.

data.title: Squash frequently during feature development
data.text: Do not wait until the end of a long feature to squash. Squash frequently as you go. It keeps the branch clean and makes review easier for your teammates.

items.question: Will squashing change my code?
items.answer: No. Squashing only changes the commit structure. The final combined commit contains all the changes from the squashed commits in the same order.

items.question: Can I squash commits on main after merging?
items.answer: Technically yes, but it is bad practice. Rewrite public history only with extreme care and coordination. Use pull request reviews and CI to ensure clean history before merging.

items.question: What is the difference between fixup and squash?
items.answer: fixup discards the secondary commit's message; squash lets you edit the combined message. fixup is for pure corrections, squash is for combining related commits.

items.question: Does --autosquash modify my todo list?
items.answer: Yes. --autosquash automatically reorders the todo list to place fixup and squash commits next to their targets, and marks them with the appropriate action.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: squash combines commits and merges their messages
fixup combines commits but discards the secondary message
--autosquash automatically positions fixup commits in the todo list
Always rewrite only local, unshared commits
Squash frequently, not just at the end of a feature
